cor-alternating-determinant-square.title: The Determinant of an Alternating Matrix Is a Square
cor-alternating-determinant-square.title_html: The Determinant of an Alternating Matrix Is a Square
cor-alternating-determinant-square.html: Let F be any field and let A∈Mn(F) be alternating. Then detA is a square in F: there is c∈F with detA=c2.

cor-alternating-even-rank.title: Alternating Matrices Are Classified by Rank
cor-alternating-even-rank.title_html: Alternating Matrices Are Classified by Rank
cor-alternating-even-rank.html:
Let F be any field and let A,B∈Mn(F) be alternating.

  1. rankA is even.
  2. A≃B if and only if rankA=rankB.
  3. There are exactly ⌊n/2⌋+1 congruence classes of alternating matrices in Mn(F), one for each even rank 0,2,4,… up to n.
  4. If n is odd, every alternating A∈Mn(F) is singular.

cor-complex-symmetric-classification.title: Classification of Complex Symmetric Matrices by Rank
cor-complex-symmetric-classification.title_html: Classification of Complex Symmetric Matrices by Rank
cor-complex-symmetric-classification.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be symmetric of rank r. Then A is congruent to Ir⊕0n−r=diag(1,…,1⏟r,0,…,0). Consequently two symmetric matrices in Mn(C) are congruent if and only if they have the same rank, and there are exactly n+1 congruence classes.

cor-real-symmetric-classification.title: Classification of Real Symmetric Matrices by Signature
cor-real-symmetric-classification.title_html: Classification of Real Symmetric Matrices by Signature
cor-real-symmetric-classification.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(R) be symmetric. Then:

  1. A is congruent to In+⊕(−In−)⊕0n0, where (n+,n−,n0) is the inertia of A, and to no other matrix of this shape;
  2. A≃B if and only if A and B have the same inertia;
  3. the number of congruence classes of symmetric matrices in Mn(R) is 12(n+1)(n+2).

cor-witt-cancellation.title: Witt’s Cancellation Theorem
cor-witt-cancellation.html:
Let charF≠2.

  1. Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on V, and let U,U′⊆V be isometric subspaces. Then U⊥β≅U′⊥β.
  2. Let (V,β) and (V′,β′) be finite-dimensional spaces with non-degenerate symmetric forms, and suppose V=U⊥W,V′=U′⊥W′. If V≅V′ and U≅U′, then W≅W′.

cor-witt-decomposition-unique.title: The Anisotropic Part Is Determined
cor-witt-decomposition-unique.html: Let charF≠2, let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on a finite-dimensional V, and let V=H1⊥⋯⊥Hm⊥V0=H1′⊥⋯⊥Hm′′⊥V0′ be two decompositions as in @thm-witt-decomposition. Then m=m′=ind(β) and V0≅V0′.

def-algebra-over-field.title: Algebra over a Field
def-algebra-over-field.html:
An algebra over F, or an F-algebra, is a vector space A over F together with a map A×A→A, written (x,y)↦xy, which is

  1. bilinear: linear in each argument with the other fixed;
  2. associative: (xy)z=x(yz) for all x,y,z∈A;
  3. unital: there is an element 1A∈A with 1Ax=x1A=x for every x∈A.

A homomorphism of F-algebras is an F-linear map φ:A→B with φ(xy)=φ(x)φ(y) for all x,y and φ(1A)=1B. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism.

def-bilinear-form.title: Bilinear Form
def-bilinear-form.html:
Let V be a vector space over a field F. A bilinear form on V is a function β:V×V→F that is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed: for all u,u′,v,v′∈V and all c∈F,

  1. β(u+u′,v)=β(u,v)+β(u′,v) and β(cu,v)=cβ(u,v);
  2. β(u,v+v′)=β(u,v)+β(u,v′) and β(u,cv)=cβ(u,v).

Equivalently, β is a 2-linear form on V in the sense of @def-multilinear-form.

def-causal-character.title: Timelike, Spacelike, Null
def-causal-character.html:
Let x∈R1,3 with x≠0. Then x is

  1. timelike if q(x)>0;
  2. null, or lightlike, if q(x)=0;
  3. spacelike if q(x)<0.

The set {x∈R1,3:q(x)=0} is the light cone. A timelike x is future-pointing if x1>0 and past-pointing if x1<0.

def-classical-groups.title: The Indefinite Orthogonal and Symplectic Groups
def-classical-groups.title_html: The Indefinite Orthogonal and Symplectic Groups
def-classical-groups.html: For p,q≥0 with p+q=n, set Ip,q:=Ip⊕(−Iq)∈Mn(R) and O(p,q):=Isom(Ip,q)={P∈Mn(R):P⊤Ip,qP=Ip,q}, the indefinite orthogonal group of signature (p,q). For m≥1 and any field F, set Sp(2m,F):=Isom(Ω2m)={P∈M2m(F):P⊤Ω2mP=Ω2m}, the symplectic group, where Ω2m is the standard alternating matrix of @eq-standard-alternating-matrix.

def-clifford-algebra.title: Clifford Algebra
def-clifford-algebra.html:
Let F be a field with charF≠2, let V be a finite-dimensional F-vector space, let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V and let q(v)=β(v,v) be its quadratic form (@def-quadratic-form). A Clifford algebra of (V,q) is a pair (C,ι), where C is an F-algebra and ι:V→C is a linear map, such that

  1. ι(v)2=q(v)1C for every v∈V;
  2. (universal property) for every F-algebra A and every linear map f:V→A with f(v)2=q(v)1A for every v∈V, there is a unique algebra homomorphism f¯:C→A with f¯∘ι=f.

We write Cl(q), or Cl(V,q), for a Clifford algebra of (V,q), and Clp,m(R) when V is the space Rp,m of @def-minkowski-space, that is, Rp+m with the real form of signature (p,m).

def-congruent.title: Congruent Matrices
def-congruent.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F). We say A is congruent to B, written A≃B, if there exists an invertible P∈Mn(F) such that B=P⊤AP.

def-darboux-basis.title: Symplectic Basis
def-darboux-basis.html: A basis of V as in @thm-symplectic-standard-form is a symplectic basis, or a Darboux basis, for the alternating form β. A non-degenerate alternating form on a finite-dimensional space is called a symplectic form, and the pair (V,β) a symplectic vector space.

def-definiteness-of-a-form.title: Definiteness of a Real Symmetric Form
def-definiteness-of-a-form.title_html: Definiteness of a Real Symmetric Form
def-definiteness-of-a-form.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V, with quadratic form q. Then β is:

  1. positive definite if q(v)>0 for every non-zero v∈V;
  2. positive semidefinite if q(v)≥0 for every v∈V;
  3. negative definite if q(v)<0 for every non-zero v∈V;
  4. negative semidefinite if q(v)≤0 for every v∈V;
  5. indefinite if there exist u,w∈V with q(u)>0 and q(w)<0.

The same five words apply to a real symmetric matrix A, through the form β(x,y)=x⊤Ay on Rn.

def-discriminant.title: Discriminant
def-discriminant.html: Let β be a non-degenerate bilinear form on an n-dimensional V. The discriminant of β is the square class of det[β]B in F×, for any ordered basis B of V.

def-form-isometry.title: Isometry of Bilinear Spaces
def-form-isometry.html:
Let β be a bilinear form on V and β′ one on V′. An isometry from (V,β) to (V′,β′) is a linear bijection σ:V→V′ with β′(σ(u),σ(v))=β(u,v)for all u,v∈V. The two spaces are isometric, written (V,β)≅(V′,β′) or just V≅V′, if such a σ exists. An isometry of (V,β) with itself is an isometry of V.

When U⊆V and U′⊆V′ are subspaces, “an isometry U→U′” always means an isometry for the restricted forms β|U×U and β′|U′×U′.

def-form-matrix.title: Matrix of a Bilinear Form
def-form-matrix.html: Let β be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V with ordered basis B=(v1,…,vn). The matrix of β with respect to B, also called its Gram matrix, is the matrix [β]B∈Mn(F) with entries ([β]B)ij:=β(vi,vj).

def-form-reflection.title: Reflection in an Anisotropic Vector
def-form-reflection.html: Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V and let w∈V be anisotropic, that is q(w)≠0. The reflection in w is the map τw:V→V,τw(v)=v−2β(v,w)q(w)w.

def-hermitian-form.title: Hermitian Form
def-hermitian-form.html: Let V be a vector space over C. A function β:V×V→C is a Hermitian form if it is linear in the first argument, and β(v,u)=β(u,v)―for all u,v∈V.

def-hessian.title: Hessian
def-hessian.html: Let f be a real-valued function on an open set U⊆Rn, twice continuously differentiable on U, and let a∈U. The Hessian of f at a is the matrix Hf(a)∈Mn(R),(Hf(a))ij=∂2f∂xi∂xj(a). A point a∈U with ∇f(a)=0 is a critical point of f.

def-hyperbolic-pair.title: Hyperbolic Pair
def-hyperbolic-pair.html: Let β be an alternating form on V. A hyperbolic pair for β is an ordered pair (u,w) of vectors of V with β(u,w)=1. Its span H=span(u,w) is called a hyperbolic plane for β.

def-hyperbolic-plane.title: Hyperbolic Pair, Hyperbolic Plane
def-hyperbolic-plane.html: Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V. A hyperbolic pair is an ordered pair (e,f) of vectors of V with q(e)=0,q(f)=0,β(e,f)=1. The subspace H=span(e,f) is then called a hyperbolic plane, and (e,f) is a hyperbolic basis of it.

def-isometry-group-of-form.title: Isometry Group of a Form
def-isometry-group-of-form.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and β a non-degenerate bilinear form on V (@def-nondegenerate). An operator T∈L(V) is an isometry of β if β(Tu,Tv)=β(u,v)for all u,v∈V, and the set of all of them is written Isom(β).

For a non-singular A∈Mn(F), the corresponding matrix group is Isom(A):={P∈Mn(F):P⊤AP=A}. When F=C and A∗=A is non-singular Hermitian, Isom(A) means instead {P:P∗AP=A}.

def-isotropic-vector.title: Isotropic and Anisotropic
def-isotropic-vector.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V with quadratic form q.

  1. A vector v∈V is isotropic if v≠0 and q(v)=0, and anisotropic if q(v)≠0.
  2. The form β is anisotropic if it has no isotropic vectors: that is, if q(v)=0 implies v=0. Otherwise β is isotropic.

def-lorentz-boost.title: Boost
def-lorentz-boost.html: For t∈R, the boost of rapidity t is Bt:=(cosh⁡tsinh⁡tsinh⁡tcosh⁡t)∈M2(R).

def-minkowski-space.title: Minkowski Space
def-minkowski-space.html: Minkowski space R1,3 is the real vector space R4 equipped with the symmetric bilinear form η(x,y):=x1y1−x2y2−x3y3−x4y4, whose quadratic form is q(x)=x12−x22−x32−x42. The first coordinate is the time coordinate and the remaining three are the space coordinates. More generally, for p,m≥0, Rp,m is Rp+m with the form whose matrix in the standard basis is Ip⊕(−Im).

def-nondegenerate.title: Non-degenerate Form
def-nondegenerate.html: A bilinear form β on V is non-degenerate if rad(β)={0}, that is, if for every non-zero v∈V there exists u∈V with β(u,v)≠0. Otherwise β is degenerate.

def-orthogonal-basis-form.title: Orthogonal Basis for a Form
def-orthogonal-basis-form.html: Let β be a bilinear form on V. Vectors u,v∈V are orthogonal with respect to β if β(u,v)=0. An ordered basis B=(v1,…,vn) of V is an orthogonal basis for β if β(vi,vj)=0whenever i≠j.

def-quadratic-form.title: Quadratic Form
def-quadratic-form.html: Let β be a bilinear form on V. The quadratic form associated with β is the function q:V→F,q(v)=β(v,v). A function q:V→F is called a quadratic form on V if q(v)=β(v,v) for some symmetric bilinear form β on V.

def-quaternions.title: The Quaternions
def-quaternions.html: Inside M2(C), regarded as an algebra over R, put i=(i00−i),j=(01−10),k=(0ii0). The quaternions H are the real span of I2,i,j,k in M2(C).

def-radical.title: Radical of a Form
def-radical.html: Let β be a bilinear form on V. The radical of β is rad(β):={v∈V:β(u,v)=0 for every u∈V}=kerRβ, a subspace of V. Its elements are the vectors that every vector is orthogonal to.

def-signature.title: Inertia and Signature
def-signature.html: Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, diagonalized in some orthogonal basis. The triple (n+,n−,n0) of numbers of positive, negative and zero diagonal entries is the inertia of β, and it is well defined by @thm-sylvester-inertia. The pair (n+,n−) is the signature of β, and n++n−=rankβ while n0=n−rankβ. The same words are used for a real symmetric matrix A, through the form β(x,y)=x⊤Ay, and we write n+(A), n−(A), n0(A).

def-symmetric-form.title: Symmetric Bilinear Form
def-symmetric-form.html: A bilinear form β:V×V→F is symmetric if β(u,v)=β(v,u) for all u,v∈V.

def-totally-isotropic-subspace.title: Totally Isotropic Subspace
def-totally-isotropic-subspace.html: A subspace W⊆V is totally isotropic for β if β(u,w)=0 for all u,w∈W; equivalently, if W⊆W⊥β. The zero subspace is totally isotropic, trivially.

def-witt-index.title: Witt Index
def-witt-index.html: Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V. The Witt index of β is ind(β):=max{dim⁡W:W⊆V totally isotropic}, the largest dimension of a totally isotropic subspace. By @prp-totally-isotropic-bound it satisfies ind(β)≤n/2, and it is 0 exactly when β is anisotropic.

eq-real-canonical-form.html: In+⊕(−In−)⊕0n0,

eq-standard-alternating-matrix.html: [β]B=Ω2m⊕0n−2m,Ω2m:=(0Im−Im0).

exm-alternating-2x2.html: Describe all alternating bilinear forms on F2, and decide which are non-degenerate.

exm-bilinear-forms-first.title: Six two-slot functions
exm-bilinear-forms-first.html:
Decide which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space over the given field.

  1. The dot product on Fn: β(x,y)=x1y1+⋯+xnyn.
  2. On Fn, for a fixed A∈Mn(F): βA(x,y)=x⊤Ay.
  3. On F2: β(x,y)=x1y2−x2y1.
  4. On R[x]≤2: β(f,g)=∫01f(t)g(t)dt.
  5. On any V: the zero function β(u,v)=0.
  6. On Rn: β(x,y)=‖x‖‖y‖, the product of the Euclidean lengths.

exm-causal-character-samples.html: Classify e1, e2, e1+e2 and (2,1,1,1) in R1,3, and decide which of them are isotropic.

exm-clifford-of-zero-space.html: Let V={0}, so q=0 and n=0. Show that (F,ι) with ι=0 is a Clifford algebra of (V,q), so that Cl(0)=F.

exm-degenerate-hessian.html: The three functions g1=x2+y4,g2=x2−y4,g3=x2 all have ∇gi(0,0)=0 and the same Hessian at the origin. What is that Hessian, and what happens at the origin in each case?

exm-elements-of-the-classical-groups.title: Members of Each Family
exm-elements-of-the-classical-groups.html:

  1. (cosh⁡tsinh⁡tsinh⁡tcosh⁡t)∈O(1,1) for every t∈R.

exm-form-in-a-new-basis.title: Killing the cross term
exm-form-in-a-new-basis.html: On R2, let β(x,y)=x1y1+2x1y2+2x2y1+x2y2, so that A=[β]E=(1221). Compute [β]B′ for B′=((1,0), (−2,1)), both by @thm-change-of-basis-form and directly from @def-form-matrix.

exm-form-matrices.title: Four Gram matrices
exm-form-matrices.html:
Compute [β]B in each case.

  1. The dot product on Fn, with B=E the standard basis.
  2. βA(x,y)=x⊤Ay on Fn, with B=E.
  3. The signed area β(x,y)=x1y2−x2y1 on F2, with B=E.
  4. β(f,g)=∫01fg on R[x]≤2, with B=(1,x,x2).

exm-inertia-by-elimination.title: A signature by symmetric elimination
exm-inertia-by-elimination.html: Find the inertia of A=(112123231), and say whether the form q(x)=x⊤Ax is positive definite.

exm-pfaffian-small.title: The Pfaffian in Sizes 2 and 4
exm-pfaffian-small.html: For n=2, A=(0a−a0),detA=a2,Pf(A)=a. For n=4, write the six independent entries as a=a12, b=a13, c=a14, d=a23, e=a24, f=a34. Expanding the 4×4 determinant gives detA=(af−be+cd)2,Pf(A)=af−be+cd. The three terms pair up {1,2}{3,4}, {1,3}{2,4} and {1,4}{2,3}: the Pfaffian sums over the ways of splitting {1,2,3,4} into two pairs, with a sign. For the matrix A of @exm-darboux-basis-4x4 this reads Pf(A)=1⋅0−2⋅1+3⋅1=1, and indeed detA=1.

exm-quadratic-form-coefficients.title_html: From a polynomial to its matrix and back
exm-quadratic-form-coefficients.html: Over Q, let q(x1,x2,x3)=2x12−x22+6x1x2−4x2x3. Find the symmetric matrix A with q(x)=x⊤Ax, and evaluate q(1,1,1) both from the polynomial and from A.

exm-radical-examples.html:

  2. β(x,y)=x1y1−x2y2 on R2.

exr-bilinear-forms-a1.title: A1
exr-bilinear-forms-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for β:V×V→F to be a bilinear form, stating both clauses in full.
  2. Define the matrix [β]B of a bilinear form with respect to an ordered basis B, and state how β(u,v) is recovered from it.

exr-bilinear-forms-b1.title: B1: Which are forms?
exr-bilinear-forms-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space. Justify your answer; for those that fail, name the clause that fails and give a witness.

  1. On R2: β(x,y)=x1y1+2x1y2−3x2y1.
  2. On R2: β(x,y)=x1y1+1.
  3. On R[x]≤2: β(f,g)=f(1)g(2)−f(0)g(0).
  4. On R2: β(x,y)=x12y1.
  5. On M2(R): β(X,Y)=tr(X⊤Y).

exr-bilinear-forms-b2.title: B2: A Gram matrix from sample values
exr-bilinear-forms-b2.title_html: B2: A Gram matrix from sample values
exr-bilinear-forms-b2.html:
On V=R[x]≤2, define β(f,g)=f(0)g(0)+f(1)g(1)+f(2)g(2).

  2. Compute β(1+x, x2−1) directly from the definition, and again from the matrix. Check that the answers agree.

exr-bilinear-forms-b3.title: B3: Two radicals
exr-bilinear-forms-b3.html: On F3, let β(x,y)=x⊤Ay with A=(123246123). Find rad(β) and the left radical, give a basis of each, and decide whether they are equal.

exr-bilinear-forms-c1.title: C1: Over \nF_2
exr-bilinear-forms-c1.title_html: C1: Over F2
exr-bilinear-forms-c1.html:
Let β(x,y)=x1y1+x2y2 on V=F22.

  2. Find every v∈V with β(v,v)=0.

exr-bilinear-forms-c2.title: C2: Orthogonal complements for a form
exr-bilinear-forms-c2.title_html: C2: Orthogonal complements for a form
exr-bilinear-forms-c2.html:
Let β be a bilinear form on a vector space V with dim⁡V=n, and for a subspace U⊆V put U⊥β:={v∈V:β(u,v)=0 for every u∈U}.

  1. Prove that U⊥β is a subspace and that dim⁡U⊥β≥n−dim⁡U.
  2. Prove that equality holds when β is non-degenerate.
  3. Give an example with dim⁡U=1 in which the inequality in (a) is strict.

Hint: consider the map V→U∗ that sends v to the restriction of β(⋅,v) to U.

exr-bilinear-forms-c3.title: C3: The evaluation pairing
exr-bilinear-forms-c3.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional and let W=V∗×V. Define β on W by β((φ,v),(ψ,w)):=ψ(v)+φ(w).

  1. Prove that β is a bilinear form on W.
  2. Prove that β is non-degenerate. Hint: the two summands of an element of the radical can be killed separately.
  3. Deduce that if v∈V satisfies φ(v)=0 for every φ∈V∗, then v=0, and name the result of Chapter 4 this recovers.

exr-clifford-algebras-a1.title: A1
exr-clifford-algebras-a1.html:
1. State the definition of an F-algebra, and give one example of dimension 1 and one of dimension 4.
  2. State the universal property (C2), with every quantifier.
  3. What is Cl(0) when V={0}, and what is its dimension?
  4. True or false: Cl0,2(R) is commutative. Justify your answer.
  5. What does this book prove about dim⁡Cl(q) when dim⁡V=3, and what does it only quote?

exr-clifford-algebras-b1.title: B1: The split case
exr-clifford-algebras-b1.html: Let V=R with q(x)=x2, the form of signature (1,0). Let A=R×R with componentwise addition and multiplication, and ι:R→A, ι(x)=(x,−x). Prove that (A,ι) is a Clifford algebra of (V,q), and state its dimension.

exr-clifford-algebras-b2.title: B2
exr-clifford-algebras-b2.html:
Work in Cl0,2(R)=H, with ι(x)=x1i+x2j. Let u=(1,2) and v=(3,−1).

  1. Compute ι(u)ι(v) and ι(v)ι(u), and verify @lem-clifford-anticommutation on this pair.
  2. Compute q(u), verify ι(u)2=q(u)1H, and write down ι(u)−1.

exr-clifford-algebras-b3.title: B3
exr-clifford-algebras-b3.html: In R0,2 let u=e1 and v=e1+e2. Compute the reflection su(v) directly from the formula in @prp-clifford-reflection, then compute −ι(u)ι(v)ι(u)−1 inside H, and check that the two agree.

exr-clifford-algebras-c1.title: C1: A Clifford algebra of matrices
exr-clifford-algebras-c1.title_html: C1: A Clifford algebra of matrices
exr-clifford-algebras-c1.html:
In M2(R) put E1=(100−1) and E2=(01−10), and let V=R2 carry the form q(x)=x12−x22 of signature (1,1), with f(x)=x1E1+x2E2.

  1. Prove that f(x)2=q(x)I2 for every x, and that (I2,E1,E2,E1E2) is a basis of M2(R).
  2. Assume a Clifford algebra (C,ι) of (V,q) exists. Deduce that C≅M2(R), and hence that dim⁡C=4.

Hint for (b): the homomorphism the universal property hands you has a surjective image; then count.

exr-clifford-algebras-c2.title: C2: Why characteristic 2 is excluded
exr-clifford-algebras-c2.html: Explain why @def-clifford-algebra assumes charF≠2, by naming the first statement of this section that fails without it and saying what replaces the missing input.

exr-congruence-a1.title: A1
exr-congruence-a1.html:
1. State the change-of-basis rule for the matrix of a bilinear form, saying which matrix P appears.
  2. Define what it means for A,B∈Mn(F) to be congruent.
  3. For each of rank, symmetry, determinant, eigenvalues and the square class of a non-zero determinant, say whether it is a congruence invariant.
  4. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: congruent matrices are similar.
  5. State the one circumstance in which a change of basis is simultaneously a similarity and a congruence.

exr-congruence-b1.title: B1: A congruence in \nQ
exr-congruence-b1.title_html: B1: A congruence in Q
exr-congruence-b1.html:
Let A=(0110) and P=(111−1), both over Q.

  1. Compute P⊤AP, and hence write down a matrix congruent to A that is diagonal.
  2. Find the eigenvalues of both matrices and compare them.
  3. Compute the discriminant of the form x⊤Ay and check that it agrees for the two matrices.

exr-congruence-b2.title: B2: A non-congruence over \nQ
exr-congruence-b2.title_html: B2: A non-congruence over Q
exr-congruence-b2.html:
1. Prove that diag(1,1) and diag(1,2) are not congruent over Q.
  2. Prove that they are congruent over R, by exhibiting P.
  3. Explain in one sentence why (a) and (b) are consistent.

exr-congruence-b3.title: B3: Completing the square, again
exr-congruence-b3.html:
On R2, let β(x,y)=x1y1−x1y2−x2y1+2x2y2.

  1. Write down A=[β]E and expand q(x)=β(x,x) as a polynomial in x1,x2.
  2. Complete the square to find a basis B′ with [β]B′=I2. Verify by computing P⊤AP.
  3. Hence find the eigenvalues of A and compare them with those of I2.

exr-congruence-c1.title: C1: Congruence versus equivalence
exr-congruence-c1.html:
1. Prove that if A≃B then A and B are equivalent in the sense of @def-equivalent-matrices.
  2. Give two matrices in M2(Q) that are equivalent but not congruent, and justify your example.
  3. Hence explain what “the congruence classes refine the equivalence classes” means, and say what extra information a congruence class carries that a rank does not.

exr-congruence-c2.title: C2: Orthogonal congruence
exr-congruence-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with multiplicity.

  1. Prove that A≃diag(λ1,…,λn).
  2. Deduce that if every λi is non-zero, then A is congruent to a diagonal matrix all of whose entries are ±1.
  3. Give two real symmetric 2×2 matrices that are congruent and have no eigenvalue in common.

Hint for (b): recall from @exm-congruence-first (b) what scaling a basis vector does to a diagonal entry.

exr-congruence-c3.title: C3: How much the discriminant sees
exr-congruence-c3.title_html: C3: How much the discriminant sees
exr-congruence-c3.html:
1. Show that C× has exactly one square class, and that R× has exactly two.
  2. List the squares in F5× and show that F5× has exactly two square classes.
  3. Hence determine, for each of C, R and F5, the largest number of pairwise non-congruent invertible matrices in Mn that the discriminant alone can distinguish.

exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title: A1
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.html:
1. Define what it means for a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space to be indefinite.
  2. State the signature condition equivalent to negative semidefiniteness, and the one equivalent to positive definiteness.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: a symmetric form that is not positive semidefinite is indefinite.
  4. Name the two results of analysis that @thm-second-derivative-test assumes, and say which part of its proof uses each.
  5. A critical point has n0=2 and n−=0. What does @thm-second-derivative-test conclude?

exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title: B1: Classify by the signature
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.html: Determine the definiteness of each of the following real symmetric matrices, and give the inertia of each. Justify your answers. A1=(2112),A2=(−122−5),A3=(1221).

exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title: B2: Critical points of a quartic
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title_html: B2: Critical points of a quartic
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.html: Find all critical points of f(x,y)=x4+y4−4xy and classify each with @thm-second-derivative-test.

exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title: C1: The signature measures positive subspaces
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title_html: C1: The signature measures positive subspaces
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, with inertia (n+,n−,n0). Call a subspace U⊆V positive if q(v)>0 for every non-zero v∈U.

  1. Prove that V has a positive subspace of dimension n+.
  2. Prove that every positive subspace has dimension at most n+. Hint: consider a subspace on which q≤0 of the largest available dimension.
  3. Hence deduce that n+ equals the largest dimension of a positive subspace, and that this gives a second proof that n+ does not depend on the orthogonal basis.

exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title: C2: A saddle the determinant hides
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.title_html: C2: A saddle the determinant hides
exr-definiteness-and-second-derivatives-.html:
Let f(x,y,z)=x2−y2−z2+xyz.

  1. Verify that the origin is a critical point and compute Hf(0) and its determinant.
  2. Classify the origin, and explain why the sign of detHf(0) alone would have been useless.
  3. Prove that no twice continuously differentiable g:R3→R has a strict local maximum at a critical point 0 with detHg(0)>0, and give a g:R2→R that does. Which feature of the dimension is responsible?

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-a1.title: A1
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for an ordered basis to be an orthogonal basis for a bilinear form β, and say what that means about [β]B.
  2. State @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable with all of its hypotheses.
  3. Which step of the proof uses charF≠2, and what exactly is divided by?
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if P⊤AP=diag(d1,…,dn), then the di are the eigenvalues of A.
  5. Describe the pair of operations that a congruence by an elementary matrix performs.

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b1.title: B1: Symmetric elimination
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b1.html: Over Q, let A=(120213031). Diagonalize A by paired row and column operations, exhibiting P and P⊤AP.

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b2.title: B2: No pivot on the diagonal
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b2.title_html: B2: No pivot on the diagonal
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b2.html:
Over Q, let A=(0110) and q(x)=2x1x2.

  1. Find a vector v with q(v)≠0, as in @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists.
  2. Diagonalize A by paired operations and exhibit P.
  3. Write q as a difference of two squares in the new coordinates.

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b3.title: B3: Reading off the rank
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b3.html: Let A∈M4(C) be symmetric with rankA=3. Write down the normal form of A under congruence, and say how many congruence classes of symmetric matrices there are in M4(C).

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c1.title: C1: Square classes over a finite field
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c1.title_html: C1: Square classes over a finite field
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c1.html:
Work over F5, whose non-zero squares are 1 and 4.

  1. Prove that the 1×1 matrices (1) and (2) are not congruent over F5.
  2. Prove that I2 and 2I2 are congruent over F5, by exhibiting a P.
  3. Explain why (a) and (b) are consistent with @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes.

Hint: for (b), look for two vectors p1,p2 with pi⋅pi=2 and p1⋅p2=0.

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c2.title: C2: Is this still true over \nF_2?
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c2.title_html: C2: Is this still true over F2?
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c2.html:
Let A=(0110) over F2, and let β(x,y)=x⊤Ay on F22.

  1. Prove that β is alternating.
  2. Prove that if P∈M2(F2) is invertible, then every diagonal entry of P⊤AP is 0.
  3. Deduce that A is congruent to no diagonal matrix except the zero matrix, and hence that @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable fails over F2.

exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c3.title: C3: Diagonalizing the restriction
exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-c3.html:
Let charF≠2, let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V, and let U⊆V be a subspace.

  1. Prove that U has an orthogonal basis for the restriction of β to U.
  2. Give an example, with dim⁡V=2, in which β is non-degenerate but its restriction to some 1-dimensional U is the zero form.
  3. Deduce that an orthogonal basis of U cannot always be extended to an orthogonal basis of V by adding vectors of U alone, and say in one sentence what @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable does guarantee instead.

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: A1
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
1. Define isotropic vector, totally isotropic subspace and hyperbolic pair.
  2. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: a non-degenerate form has no isotropic vectors.
  3. What is the Witt index of a positive definite form on a space of dimension n? Of a form of signature (4,4)?
  4. State the Gram matrix of a hyperbolic plane in a hyperbolic basis, and say why it shows the restricted form is non-degenerate.
  5. Which hypothesis of @lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic fails for the form q(x)=x12 on R2 at the isotropic vector e2?

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: B1: Find the isotropic vectors
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
For each of the following real quadratic forms, find all isotropic vectors, give the signature, and state the Witt index.

  1. q(x1,x2)=x12+2x1x2 on R2.
  2. q(x1,x2,x3)=x1x2 on R3. (Is this form non-degenerate?)
  3. q(x1,x2,x3)=x12+x22+x32 on R3.

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: B2: Build a hyperbolic basis
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
1. For q(x1,x2)=x12+x22 on C2, find a hyperbolic pair.
  2. For q(x1,x2,x3)=x12+x22−x32 on R3, find a hyperbolic pair (e,f) with e=e1+e3, and identify the anisotropic part span(e,f)⊥β.

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: B3: A totally isotropic subspace of the largest size
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title_html: B3: A totally isotropic subspace of the largest size
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
Let q(x)=x1x4+x2x3 on R4.

  1. Write down the Gram matrix and verify that β is non-degenerate.
  2. Exhibit a totally isotropic subspace of dimension 2, and explain why none of dimension 3 exists.
  3. Determine the signature of q and confirm the Witt index by @prp-witt-index-real-complex (a).

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: C1: Isotropy makes the form surjective
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title_html: C1: Isotropy makes the form surjective
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on V over a field F with charF≠2.

  1. Prove that if β has an isotropic vector, then q:V→F is surjective.
  2. Deduce that if some c∈F is not of the form q(v), then β is anisotropic.
  3. Use (b) to show that the form q(x1,x2)=x12+x22 on F32 is anisotropic, and give its Witt index.

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: C2: A maximal totally isotropic subspace and its complement
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title_html: C2: A maximal totally isotropic subspace and its complement
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
Let β be non-degenerate symmetric on V with dim⁡V=n, and let W⊆V be totally isotropic with dim⁡W=ind(β)=m.

  1. Prove that dim⁡W⊥β=n−m and W⊆W⊥β.
  2. Prove that the form induced by β on the quotient W⊥β/W is well defined and anisotropic. Hint: a coset with an isotropic representative would enlarge W.
  3. Deduce that n−2m=dim⁡(W⊥β/W) agrees with the dimension of the anisotropic part in @thm-witt-decomposition.

exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.title: C3: Where characteristic 2 breaks
exr-isotropic-vectors-and-hyperbolic-pla.html:
Work over F2 and let β be the dot product on F22, with Gram matrix I2.

  1. Verify that β is symmetric and non-degenerate, and find all v with q(v)=0.
  2. Show that β has a vector with q(v)=0 and v≠0 that lies in no hyperbolic plane, and identify which line of the proof of @lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic fails.
  3. Explain in one sentence why the third description of “totally isotropic” given after @def-totally-isotropic-subspace is unavailable here.

exr-minkowski-space-a1.title: A1
exr-minkowski-space-a1.html:
1. State the sign convention used in this section, give the matrix of η in the standard basis, and say what its signature and inertia are.
  2. Define timelike, null and spacelike, and say which earlier notion the word “null” renames.
  3. True or false: the sum of two spacelike vectors is spacelike. Justify your answer.
  4. Write down detBt and Bt−1, and say which row of the comparison table each answer sits in.
  5. True or false: O(1,1) is abelian. Justify your answer.

exr-minkowski-space-b1.title: B1
exr-minkowski-space-b1.html: Determine which of the following lie in O(1,1). For each one that does, give its rapidity t and the signs ε,μ of @thm-lorentz-boost-form. Justify your answer. A1=(5/34/34/35/3),A2=(2112),A3=(5/3−4/34/3−5/3).

exr-minkowski-space-b2.title: B2
exr-minkowski-space-b2.html:
1. Classify x=(3,1,2,2), y=(1,0,1,0) and z=(0,1,1,1) in R1,3 as timelike, null or spacelike.
  2. The vector y is null. Find a w∈R1,3 such that (y,w) is a basis of a hyperbolic plane, that is, q(w)=0 and η(y,w)=1.

exr-minkowski-space-b3.title: B3
exr-minkowski-space-b3.html: Let x=(5,3,0,0) and y=(13,12,0,0) in R1,3. Compute τ(x), τ(y), η(x,y) and τ(x+y), and check @lem-reversed-cauchy-schwarz and @thm-reversed-triangle-inequality on this pair. Is either inequality an equality?

exr-minkowski-space-c1.title: C1
exr-minkowski-space-c1.html:
For t∈R put v(t)=tanh⁡t=sinh⁡t/cosh⁡t.

  1. Prove that v:R→(−1,1) is a bijection, and that Bte1 is a positive multiple of (1,v(t),0,0) read in R1,1.
  2. Hence deduce that v(s+t)=v(s)+v(t)1+v(s)v(t), and say which part of @thm-lorentz-boost-form does the work.

exr-minkowski-space-c2.title: C2
exr-minkowski-space-c2.html:
1. Prove that {Pe1:P∈O(1,1)} is the set of all x∈R1,1 with q(x)=1, and that this set is unbounded.
  2. Deduce that no bound |pij|≤c holds for all P∈O(1,1), and contrast this with O(2), where |pij|≤1 always. Which hypothesis of Chapter 10’s O(2) theory is responsible?

exr-minkowski-space-c3.title: C3
exr-minkowski-space-c3.html:
The Quick check above showed that R1,3 has no plane on which the form vanishes identically. Show that R2,2 does have one, by exhibiting two vectors that span it, and reconcile the two answers with @thm-witt-decomposition.

Hint: pair each positive coordinate with a negative one.

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-a1.title: A1
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-a1.html:
1. Define the inertia and the signature of a real symmetric matrix.
  2. State @thm-sylvester-inertia, with all hypotheses.
  3. Which part of the inertia is already an invariant before the law of inertia is proved, and by which earlier result?
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: congruent real symmetric matrices have the same trace.
  5. Explain in one sentence why an orthogonal change of basis lets the spectral theorem compute an inertia.

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b1.title: B1: Signatures by elimination
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b1.html:
Find the inertia of each of the following real symmetric matrices by paired row and column operations. Do not compute any eigenvalues.

  1. A=(120213031).
  2. B=(011101110).
  3. C=(1224).

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b2.title: B2: Which of these are congruent?
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b2.title_html: B2: Which of these are congruent?
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b2.html: Sort the following real symmetric matrices into congruence classes, justifying each answer. A1=diag(1,1,−1),A2=diag(5,2,−7),A3=diag(1,−1,−1), A4=(010100001),A5=(20000000−3).

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b3.title: B3: Inertia from a characteristic polynomial
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b3.title_html: B3: Inertia from a characteristic polynomial
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-b3.html:
Let A∈M3(R) be symmetric with det(xI−A)=x3−2x2−5x+6.

  1. Find the inertia of A.
  2. Is A congruent to diag(1,1,−1)? Is it similar to it?

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c1.title: C1: An intrinsic description of n_+
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c1.title_html: C1: An intrinsic description of n+
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c1.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, with quadratic form q. Call a subspace U⊆V positive if q(v)>0 for every v∈U with v≠0.

  1. Prove that n+ is the largest dimension of a positive subspace of V.
  2. Deduce @thm-sylvester-inertia again from (a), in two lines.
  3. State and prove the corresponding description of n−.

Hint: for (a), use an orthogonal basis to produce one positive subspace of dimension n+, and the dimension formula to rule out a larger one.

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c2.title: C2: Congruence cannot be read off the eigenvalues, and inertia can
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c2.title_html: C2: Congruence cannot be read off the eigenvalues, and inertia can
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c2.html:
1. Give two real symmetric 2×2 matrices that are congruent but have no eigenvalue in common.
  2. Prove that if A and B are real symmetric and similar, then they are congruent.
  3. Give two real symmetric 2×2 matrices that are congruent but not similar, so that the converse of (b) fails.

exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c3.title: C3: Inertia of a block matrix
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c3.title_html: C3: Inertia of a block matrix
exr-sylvesters-law-of-inertia-c3.html:
Let A∈Mm(R) and B∈Mk(R) be symmetric. Let also D∈Mn(R) be symmetric and invertible, let b∈Rn, let c∈R, and put M=(Dbb⊤c)∈Mn+1(R).

  1. Prove that the inertia of A⊕B is the entrywise sum of the inertias of A and B.
  2. Prove that M is congruent to D⊕(c−b⊤D−1b).
  3. Hence find the inertia of M when D=diag(1,−1), b=(1,1) and c=0.

Hint: for (b), the congruence is the block elimination of Chapter 7, and the leftover scalar is a Schur complement.

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-a1.title: A1
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for a bilinear form β on V to be symmetric, alternating and skew-symmetric.
  2. State the relationship between alternating and skew-symmetric forms, including the exact role of the characteristic.
  3. Write down the matrix condition, in a fixed basis, for each of the three notions in (a).
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: over Q, a bilinear form is determined by the function v↦β(v,v).
  5. Why is a Hermitian form not an example of @def-bilinear-form?

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b1.title: B1: Determine which of the following
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b1.title_html: B1: Determine which of the following
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b1.html:
Over Q, with V=Q2 and x=(x1,x2), y=(y1,y2), determine for each of the following bilinear forms whether it is symmetric, whether it is alternating, and whether it is skew-symmetric. Justify each answer.

  1. β(x,y)=x1y1−x2y2.
  2. β(x,y)=3x1y2−3x2y1.
  3. β(x,y)=x1y2+2x2y1.
  4. β(x,y)=0.

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b2.title: B2: Polarizing a quadratic form
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b2.html:
Over R, let q(x1,x2,x3)=x12+4x1x2−2x2x3+5x32.

  1. Find the symmetric matrix A with q(x)=x⊤Ax.
  2. Compute β(e1+e2,e3) directly from A, and again from the polarization formula 12(q(u+v)−q(u)−q(v)).

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b3.title: B3: Splitting a form
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-b3.html: Let A=(15−14) over Q, and let β(x,y)=x⊤Ay. Write β=βs+βa as in @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition, giving the matrix of each part, and verify that β and βs have the same quadratic form.

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c1.title: C1: Is this still true over \nF_2?
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c1.title_html: C1: Is this still true over F2?
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c1.html:
Let V be a vector space over F2 with dim⁡V=n≥1.

  1. Prove that every alternating bilinear form on V is symmetric.
  2. Prove that the alternating forms on V form a subspace of the space of all bilinear forms, and compute its dimension.
  3. Deduce that for n=2 there is exactly one non-zero alternating form on V, and write down its matrix.

Hint: for (b), use @prp-alternating-form-matrix.

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c2.title: C2: How much of a form does q see?
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c2.title_html: C2: How much of a form does q see?
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c2.html:
Let charF≠2 and let β be any bilinear form on V, with q(v)=β(v,v).

  1. Prove that two bilinear forms have the same quadratic form if and only if their difference is alternating.
  2. Deduce that the set of bilinear forms with a given quadratic form q contains exactly one symmetric form.
  3. For dim⁡V=n, how many bilinear forms share a given quadratic form when F=F3?

exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c3.title: C3: A Hermitian form is a real symmetric form in disguise
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c3.title_html: C3: A Hermitian form is a real symmetric form in disguise
exr-symmetric-alternating-hermitian-c3.html:
Let β be a Hermitian form on Cn with matrix A=A∗ as in @prp-hermitian-form-matrix, and regard Cn as a real vector space of dimension 2n by forgetting multiplication by i.

  1. Prove that τ(u,v)=Reβ(u,v) is a symmetric R-bilinear form on that real space, with τ(v,v)=β(v,v).
  2. Prove that ω(u,v)=Imβ(u,v) is an alternating R-bilinear form.
  3. For n=1 and A=(1), write both τ and ω as explicit forms on R2.

exr-symplectic-forms-a1.title: A1
exr-symplectic-forms-a1.html:
1. Define a hyperbolic pair for an alternating form, and say why its two vectors are automatically linearly independent.
  2. State @thm-symplectic-standard-form, and say which hypothesis on F it needs.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct: every skew-symmetric matrix over every field has even rank. Justify your answer.
  4. Why can an alternating form never have a diagonal Gram matrix, unless the form is zero?
  5. How many congruence classes of alternating matrices are there in M5(R)? In M5(F7)?

exr-symplectic-forms-b1.title: B1: A symplectic basis
exr-symplectic-forms-b1.html: Let β(x,y)=x⊤By on Q4, with B=(00110021−1−200−1−100). Find a symplectic basis for β and an invertible P∈M4(Q) with P⊤BP=Ω4.

exr-symplectic-forms-b2.title: B2: Pfaffians and determinants
exr-symplectic-forms-b2.html: For each matrix below, compute the Pfaffian using the formula of @exm-pfaffian-small, and verify that its square is the determinant. A1=(0201−20100−103−10−30),A2=(0111−1011−1−101−1−1−10). Hence write down, for each, an invertible matrix congruence class in the sense of @cor-alternating-even-rank.

exr-symplectic-forms-b3.title: B3: Determine which of the following
exr-symplectic-forms-b3.title_html: B3: Determine which of the following
exr-symplectic-forms-b3.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are alternating, and for those that are, give the rank and the standard form Ω2m⊕0n−2m it is congruent to. Justify your answer.

  1. (05−50) over Q.
  2. (0110) over Q.
  3. (0110) over F2.
  4. The 5×5 matrix with aij=j−i over Q.

exr-symplectic-forms-c1.title: C1: Lagrangian subspaces
exr-symplectic-forms-c1.html:
Let β be a symplectic form on V with dim⁡V=2m (@def-darboux-basis), and call a subspace U⊆V totally isotropic if β(u,u′)=0 for all u,u′∈U.

  1. Prove that span(u1,…,um) is totally isotropic, for any symplectic basis.
  2. Prove that every totally isotropic subspace satisfies dim⁡U≤m.
  3. Deduce that a symplectic form on a space of dimension 2m has a totally isotropic subspace of dimension exactly m, and no larger one. (These are the Lagrangian subspaces.)

Hint for (b): compare U with U⊥β of @exr-bilinear-forms-c2.

exr-symplectic-forms-c2.title: C2: The inverse of an alternating matrix
exr-symplectic-forms-c2.title_html: C2: The inverse of an alternating matrix
exr-symplectic-forms-c2.html:
Let F be any field.

  1. Prove that every alternating matrix of odd size over F is singular, without using determinants.
  2. Let A∈Mn(F) be alternating and invertible. Prove that A−1 is alternating.

Hint for (b): the adjugate. The (i,i) entry of adjA is a minor of A of size n−1.

exr-symplectic-forms-c3.title: C3: Counting over a finite field
exr-symplectic-forms-c3.title_html: C3: Counting over a finite field
exr-symplectic-forms-c3.html:
Let q be a power of an odd prime.

  1. How many alternating bilinear forms are there on Fq2m? How many symmetric ones?
  2. How many of the alternating forms on Fq2 are non-degenerate, and how many congruence classes do they fall into?
  3. How many of the symmetric forms on Fq1 are non-degenerate, and how many congruence classes do they fall into? Hint: the squaring map Fq×→Fq× has kernel {1,−1}.
  4. Explain in one or two sentences why the answers to (b) and (c) differ, in terms of what a change of basis can do to the single free parameter in each case.

exr-the-classical-groups-a1.title: A1
exr-the-classical-groups-a1.html:
1. Define Isom(A) for a non-singular A∈Mn(F), and explain why its elements are automatically invertible.
  2. Which form does O(p,q) preserve, and which does Sp(2m,F) preserve?
  3. Determine whether the following is correct: if A≃B, then Isom(A)=Isom(B). Justify your answer.
  4. State what is known here about detP for P∈Sp(2m,F), distinguishing what is proved from what is only recorded.
  5. In the parameter count, what exactly does the word “dimension” mean, and what is not being claimed?

exr-the-classical-groups-b1.title: B1: Determine which of the following
exr-the-classical-groups-b1.title_html: B1: Determine which of the following
exr-the-classical-groups-b1.html:
For each matrix, determine whether it lies in O(2), in O(1,1), in Sp(2,R) — where the relevant forms are I2, I1,1=diag(1,−1) and Ω2 — listing all that apply. Justify each answer.

  1. (100−1).
  2. (0−110).
  3. (3001/3).
  4. (5/34/34/35/3).

exr-the-classical-groups-b2.title: B2: A symplectic matrix of size four
exr-the-classical-groups-b2.title_html: B2: A symplectic matrix of size four
exr-the-classical-groups-b2.html:
Let M=(1201) and S=(0110), and put P1=(M00(M⊤)−1),P2=(I2S0I2).

  1. Write out P1 explicitly and verify P1∈Sp(4,Q) directly from the definition.
  2. Explain why P1P2∈Sp(4,Q) without computing the product.
  3. Compute detP1 and detP2, and check them against @thm-classical-group-determinants.

exr-the-classical-groups-b3.title: B3: Counting parameters
exr-the-classical-groups-b3.html:
1. Compute the expected dimensions of O(4), O(2,2), U(3) and Sp(4,R).
  2. For which n and m do O(n) and Sp(2m,R) have the same expected dimension? Solve the resulting equation.
  3. The group SO(n) is cut out of O(n) by the single equation detP=1. Why does this not reduce the expected dimension by one?

exr-the-classical-groups-c1.title: C1: Isometries of a degenerate form
exr-the-classical-groups-c1.title_html: C1: Isometries of a degenerate form
exr-the-classical-groups-c1.html:
Let A=(1000)∈M2(R) and let G={P∈M2(R):P⊤AP=A}, the set produced by dropping the non-degeneracy hypothesis from @def-isometry-group-of-form.

  1. Determine G explicitly.
  2. Exhibit an element of G that is not invertible, and explain which step of the proof of @thm-classical-groups-are-groups it defeats.
  3. Prove that the invertible elements of G do form a group.

exr-the-classical-groups-c2.title: C2: The symplectic group of a two-dimensional form, revisited
exr-the-classical-groups-c2.title_html: C2: The symplectic group of a two-dimensional form, revisited
exr-the-classical-groups-c2.html:
Let F be any field and let β be a non-degenerate alternating form on a two-dimensional vector space V over F.

  1. Prove that Isom(β)={T∈L(V):detT=1}.
  2. Deduce that for F=F2 the group Sp(2,F2) has exactly 6 elements, and that Sp(2,F2)=GL2(F2).
  3. Is Sp(2,F3)=GL2(F3)? Justify your answer by a count.

Hint for (b) and (c): count the invertible matrices over Fq by choosing the columns in turn.

exr-the-classical-groups-c3.title: C3: Bounded and unbounded
exr-the-classical-groups-c3.html:
1. Prove that every entry of a matrix P∈O(n) satisfies |pij|≤1.
  2. Prove that for every n≥2 and every real M, the group O(n−1,1) contains a matrix with an entry larger than M.
  3. Explain in two sentences why (a) and (b) together make it plausible that O(n) is compact and O(n−1,1) is not, and say precisely what has and has not been proved.

exr-witts-theorems-a1.title: A1
exr-witts-theorems-a1.html:
1. State Witt’s extension theorem, with all its hypotheses.
  2. Define the reflection τw and say which vectors it fixes.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if U⊆V and U′⊆V′ are isometric subspaces of non-degenerate spaces, then U⊥ and U′⊥ are isometric.
  4. Where is charF≠2 used in the proof of @thm-witt-extension?
  5. Two real non-degenerate forms of dimension 6 both have Witt index 2. Must they be isometric?

exr-witts-theorems-b1.title: B1: Extend an isometry by hand
exr-witts-theorems-b1.title_html: B1: Extend an isometry by hand
exr-witts-theorems-b1.html:
Let V=R3 with q(x)=x12+x22−x32, let U=span(e1), U′=span(e2), and let σ(e1)=e2.

  1. Verify that σ is an isometry of U onto U′.
  2. Extend σ to an isometry of V, and write down its matrix in the standard basis.
  3. Determine U⊥β and U′⊥β and exhibit the isometry between them produced by your extension.

exr-witts-theorems-b2.title: B2: Cancel a hyperbolic plane
exr-witts-theorems-b2.html:
Let H denote a hyperbolic plane over R, and let A and B be non-degenerate real spaces with forms, with dim⁡A=dim⁡B=3. Suppose H⊥A≅H⊥B.

  1. Prove that A≅B.
  2. If A has signature (2,1), what is the signature of B?
  3. Does A⊥B≅A⊥B with A≅A allow us to conclude B≅B? Say which part of @cor-witt-cancellation is being used and why the statement is not vacuous.

exr-witts-theorems-b3.title: B3: Reflections in an indefinite space
exr-witts-theorems-b3.title_html: B3: Reflections in an indefinite space
exr-witts-theorems-b3.html:
In R2 with q(x)=x12−x22:

  1. Compute the matrix of τe1 and of τe2 in the standard basis, and check each satisfies P⊤AP=A with A=diag(1,−1).
  2. Explain why τv is undefined for v=(1,1), and say what fails.
  3. Find an isometry carrying (1,0) to (−1,0) and one carrying (2,3) to (−2,3). (Check the values of q first.)

exr-witts-theorems-c1.title: C1: Inertia from cancellation
exr-witts-theorems-c1.html:
Work over R and let V be an n-dimensional space with a non-degenerate symmetric form.

  1. Prove that if Rp,q denotes Rp+q with the form x12+⋯+xp2−xp+12−⋯−xp+q2, then Rp,q≅Rp′,q′ forces p=p′ and q=q′, using only @cor-witt-cancellation and @prp-witt-index-real-complex.
  2. Explain in one sentence how this compares with the proof of @thm-sylvester-inertia in Section 5.

exr-witts-theorems-c2.title: C2: The isometry group acts transitively
exr-witts-theorems-c2.title_html: C2: The isometry group acts transitively
exr-witts-theorems-c2.html:
Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on V, with charF≠2, and let G be the group of isometries of V.

  1. Prove that if q(u)=q(u′)≠0 then some φ∈G has φ(u)=u′.
  2. Prove that if u and u′ are both isotropic and non-zero, then some φ∈G has φ(u)=u′. Hint: an isotropic line is a one-dimensional subspace on which the form is zero.
  3. Deduce that G acts transitively on each “level set” {v≠0:q(v)=c} for c≠0, and on the set of non-zero isotropic vectors.

exr-witts-theorems-c3.title: C3: What extension does not say
exr-witts-theorems-c3.title_html: C3: What extension does not say
exr-witts-theorems-c3.html:
1. Give an example of a non-degenerate (V,β) and subspaces U,U′ of the same dimension that are not isometric, and say why @thm-witt-extension does not apply.
  2. Let β be non-degenerate on V and let U⊆V be totally isotropic with dim⁡U=ind(β). Prove that any two such U are carried onto one another by an isometry of V.
  3. Deduce that all maximal totally isotropic subspaces of a non-degenerate space have the same dimension, and compare with @prp-totally-isotropic-bound.

lem-alternating-hyperbolic-pair.title: Peeling Off a Hyperbolic Plane
lem-alternating-hyperbolic-pair.html:
Let β be an alternating form on a finite-dimensional V, and suppose β≠0.

  1. There is a hyperbolic pair (u,w) for β.
  2. For any such pair, with H=span(u,w) and H⊥β={v∈V:β(u,v)=β(w,v)=0}, we have V=H⊕H⊥β and dim⁡H⊥β=dim⁡V−2.
  3. rad(β)=rad(β|H⊥β). In particular, if β is non-degenerate then so is its restriction to H⊥β.

lem-anisotropic-vector-exists.title: A Non-Zero Form Is Non-Zero Somewhere on the Diagonal
lem-anisotropic-vector-exists.title_html: A Non-Zero Form Is Non-Zero Somewhere on the Diagonal
lem-anisotropic-vector-exists.html: Let charF≠2 and let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V with β≠0. Then there exists v∈V with q(v)≠0.

lem-clifford-anticommutation.title: The Anticommutation Relation
lem-clifford-anticommutation.html: Let (C,ι) be a Clifford algebra of (V,q). Then for all u,v∈V, ι(u)ι(v)+ι(v)ι(u)=2β(u,v)1C. In particular ι(u) and ι(v) anticommute whenever β(u,v)=0.

lem-definite-form-bounded-below.title: A Positive Definite Form Is Bounded Below by a Multiple of the Norm Squared
lem-definite-form-bounded-below.title_html:
A Positive Definite Form Is Bounded Below by a Multiple of the Norm
Squared
lem-definite-form-bounded-below.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric and positive definite, and let λ be its smallest eigenvalue. Then λ>0 and x⊤Ax ≥ λ‖x‖2for every x∈Rn.

lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic.title: Every Isotropic Vector Lies in a Hyperbolic Plane
lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic.title_html: Every Isotropic Vector Lies in a Hyperbolic Plane
lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic.html: Let charF≠2, let β be a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form on V, and let e∈V be isotropic. Then there is f∈V such that (e,f) is a hyperbolic pair. In particular e lies in a hyperbolic plane H=span(e,f), and β|H is non-degenerate.

lem-perp-dimension.title: Dimension of an Orthogonal Complement
lem-perp-dimension.html: Let β be a non-degenerate bilinear form on V with dim⁡V=n, and let U⊆V be a subspace. Then U⊥β is a subspace of V, and dim⁡U⊥β=n−dim⁡U.

lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic.title: Moving One Anisotropic Vector to Another
lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic.title_html: Moving One Anisotropic Vector to Another
lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic.html: Let charF≠2, let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V, and let u,u′∈V satisfy q(u)=q(u′)≠0. Then there is an isometry ρ of V with ρ(u)=u′, and ρ may be taken to be a reflection or a product of two reflections.

lem-reversed-cauchy-schwarz.title: Reversed Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
lem-reversed-cauchy-schwarz.html: Let x,y∈R1,3 be timelike and both future-pointing. Then η(x,y)≥τ(x)τ(y)>0, with equality if and only if y=λx for some λ>0.

prp-alternating-form-matrix.title: Alternation and Skewness in the Matrix
prp-alternating-form-matrix.title_html: Alternation and Skewness in the Matrix
prp-alternating-form-matrix.html:
Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of V and A=[β]B. Then:

  1. β is skew-symmetric if and only if A⊤=−A;
  2. β is alternating if and only if A⊤=−A and aii=0 for every i.

prp-clifford-reflection.title: Reflections Are Conjugations
prp-clifford-reflection.html: Let (C,ι) be a Clifford algebra of (V,q) and let u∈V with q(u)≠0. Then ι(u) is invertible in C, with inverse q(u)−1ι(u), and for every v∈V, −ι(u)ι(v)ι(u)−1=ι(su(v)),su(v):=v−2β(u,v)q(u)u. The map su fixes {v:β(u,v)=0} pointwise, sends u to −u, and satisfies q(su(v))=q(v).

prp-clifford-spanning.title: The Clifford Algebra Is Spanned by Sorted Products
prp-clifford-spanning.title_html: The Clifford Algebra Is Spanned by Sorted Products
prp-clifford-spanning.html: Let (C,ι) be a Clifford algebra of (V,q), where dim⁡V=n and charF≠2, and let (e1,…,en) be an orthogonal basis of V for β. Then C is spanned over F by the 2n products ι(ei1)ι(ei2)⋯ι(eik),1≤i1<i2<⋯<ik≤n, one for each subset {i1,…,ik} of {1,…,n}, the empty product being 1C. In particular dimF⁡C≤2n.

prp-clifford-uniqueness.title: Uniqueness of the Clifford Algebra
prp-clifford-uniqueness.html: Let (C,ι) and (C′,ι′) both be Clifford algebras of (V,q). Then there is a unique algebra isomorphism φ:C→C′ with φ∘ι=ι′.

prp-congruence-equivalence.title: Congruence is an equivalence relation
prp-congruence-equivalence.html: Congruence is an equivalence relation on Mn(F) (@def-equivalence-relation).

prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry.title: Congruence preserves the symmetry type
prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with B=P⊤AP for an invertible P.

  1. If A⊤=A, then B⊤=B.
  2. If A⊤=−A, then B⊤=−B.
  3. If A⊤=−A and every diagonal entry of A is 0, the same holds for B.

Each implication is an equivalence, since congruence is symmetric (@prp-congruence-equivalence).

prp-congruent-forms-conjugate-groups.title: Congruence Conjugates the Isometry Group
prp-congruent-forms-conjugate-groups.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be non-singular with B=Q⊤AQ for an invertible Q (@def-congruent). Then Isom(B)=Q−1Isom(A)Q, so the two groups are conjugate subgroups of GLn(F); in particular they are isomorphic as groups, by P↦QPQ−1.

prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms.title: Chapter 12’s Tests, in the Language of Forms
prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms.title_html: Chapter 12’s Tests, in the Language of Forms
prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on an n-dimensional real vector space, A=[β]B its matrix in any basis, and Ak the top-left k×k corner of A. Then:

  1. β is positive definite ⟺ every eigenvalue of A is positive ⟺ detAk>0 for k=1,…,n;
  2. β is negative definite ⟺ every eigenvalue of A is negative ⟺ (−1)kdetAk>0 for k=1,…,n.

prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes.title: Diagonal Entries Are Defined Only up to Squares
prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes.title_html: Diagonal Entries Are Defined Only up to Squares
prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes.html: Let B=(v1,…,vn) be an orthogonal basis for β with di=q(vi), and let t1,…,tn∈F be non-zero. Then (t1v1,…,tnvn) is again an orthogonal basis for β, with diagonal entries ti2di.

prp-form-reflection-properties.title: Reflections Are Involutive Isometries
prp-form-reflection-properties.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V and w∈V anisotropic. Then τw is linear, and:

  1. τw(w)=−w, and τw(v)=v for every v with β(v,w)=0;
  2. τw∘τw=idV; in particular τw is bijective;
  3. β(τwu,τwv)=β(u,v) for all u,v∈V.

Hence τw is an isometry of V.

prp-form-symmetry-matrix.title: Symmetry Is Visible in the Matrix
prp-form-symmetry-matrix.title_html: Symmetry Is Visible in the Matrix
prp-form-symmetry-matrix.html: Let B be a basis of V and A=[β]B. Then β is symmetric if and only if A⊤=A.

prp-hermitian-form-matrix.title: Hermitian Forms and Hermitian Matrices
prp-hermitian-form-matrix.html: Let β be linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of V, and let A be the matrix with entries aij=β(vj,vi). Then β is Hermitian if and only if A∗=A, and in that case β(u,v)=[v]B∗A[u]B.

prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible.title: Non-degeneracy is invertibility of the Gram matrix
prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible.title_html: Non-degeneracy is invertibility of the Gram matrix
prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible.html:
Let β be a bilinear form on an n-dimensional V with ordered basis B, and put A=[β]B. Then:

  1. A is the matrix of Rβ from the basis B to the dual basis B∗; that is, A=[Rβ]BB∗.
  2. dim⁡rad(β)=n−rankA.
  3. The following are equivalent: β is non-degenerate; A is invertible; Rβ is an isomorphism V→V∗.

prp-nondegenerate-restriction-splits.title: A Non-degenerate Subspace Splits Off
prp-nondegenerate-restriction-splits.html: Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on V with dim⁡V=n, and let U⊆V be a subspace such that β|U×U is non-degenerate. Then V=U⊥U⊥β, and β restricted to U⊥β is non-degenerate.

prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity.title: An orthogonal change of basis is both
prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity.title_html: An orthogonal change of basis is both
prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity.html: Let A∈Mn(R) and Q∈O(n). Then Q⊤AQ=Q−1AQ, so this matrix is at once congruent and similar to A. Consequently, if A is symmetric, then A is congruent to the diagonal matrix D of its eigenvalues, listed with multiplicity in any prescribed order.

prp-totally-isotropic-bound.title: Half the Dimension, at Most
prp-totally-isotropic-bound.html: Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on V with dim⁡V=n, and let W⊆V be totally isotropic. Then dim⁡W≤n/2.

prp-witt-index-counts-planes.title: The Number of Hyperbolic Planes Is the Witt Index
prp-witt-index-counts-planes.title_html: The Number of Hyperbolic Planes Is the Witt Index
prp-witt-index-counts-planes.html: In any decomposition V=H1⊥⋯⊥Hm⊥V0 as in @thm-witt-decomposition, m=ind(β). In particular m is the same for every such decomposition, and so is dim⁡V0=n−2m.

prp-witt-index-real-complex.title: The Witt Index over the Reals and the Complexes
prp-witt-index-real-complex.title_html: The Witt Index over the Reals and the Complexes
prp-witt-index-real-complex.html:
1. Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on a real V with signature (n+,n−) (@def-signature), so n++n−=n. Then ind(β)=min(n+,n−), and the anisotropic part has dimension |n+−n−| and is definite.
  2. Let β be a non-degenerate symmetric form on a complex V with dim⁡V=n. Then ind(β)=⌊n/2⌋. In particular every such form with n≥2 has an isotropic vector, and the anisotropic part has dimension 0 or 1.

thm-alternating-vs-skew.title: Alternating Versus Skew-Symmetric
thm-alternating-vs-skew.html:
Let F be a field and let V be a vector space over F.

  1. Every alternating bilinear form on V is skew-symmetric. No hypothesis on F or on V is needed.
  2. If charF≠2, every skew-symmetric bilinear form on V is alternating. Again V is arbitrary.
  3. If charF=2 and V≠{0}, there is a skew-symmetric bilinear form on V that is not alternating.

So the converse of (a) holds if and only if charF≠2.

thm-change-of-basis-form.title: Change of Basis for a Form
thm-change-of-basis-form.title_html: Change of Basis for a Form
thm-change-of-basis-form.html: Let β be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V, let B and B′ be ordered bases of V, and let P=[id]B′B be the change-of-coordinates matrix from B′ to B. Then [β]B′=P⊤[β]BP.

thm-classical-group-determinants.title: Determinants in the Classical Groups
thm-classical-group-determinants.html:
1. Let F be any field and A∈Mn(F) non-singular. Then detP=±1 for every P∈Isom(A). In particular detP=±1 for P∈O(p,q), and both signs occur when n≥1.
  2. If A∈Mn(C) is Hermitian and non-singular, then |detP|=1 for every P∈Isom(A); in particular for P∈U(n).
  3. Sp(2,F)=SL2(F). In particular every P∈Sp(2,F) has detP=1 exactly, and −1 does not occur.

thm-classical-groups-are-groups.title: Isometry Groups Are Groups
thm-classical-groups-are-groups.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be non-singular. Then every P∈Isom(A) is invertible, and Isom(A) is a subgroup of GLn(F). The same holds for Isom(β) inside the group of invertible operators on V, and for the Hermitian version.

thm-clifford-dimension.title: Dimension of a Clifford Algebra
thm-clifford-dimension.html: Let charF≠2, let dim⁡V=n, and let (C,ι) be a Clifford algebra of (V,q). Then the 2n sorted products of @prp-clifford-spanning form a basis of C, so dimF⁡C=2n. In particular ι is injective.

thm-congruence-determinant-class.title: Congruence changes the determinant by a square
thm-congruence-determinant-class.title_html: Congruence changes the determinant by a square
thm-congruence-determinant-class.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) with B=P⊤AP for an invertible P. Then detB=(detP)2detA, with detP≠0. In particular detA=0 if and only if detB=0, and when they are non-zero, detB=c2detA for some c∈F∖{0}.

thm-congruence-preserves-rank.title: Congruence preserves rank
thm-congruence-preserves-rank.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A≃B. Then rankA=rankB. Consequently, whether the associated form is non-degenerate is a property of the congruence class, and it is legitimate to speak of the rank of a bilinear form, meaning the rank of its matrix in any basis.

thm-definiteness-by-signature.title: Definiteness Is the Signature
thm-definiteness-by-signature.html:
Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, with inertia (n+,n−,n0) (@def-signature). Then:

  1. β is positive definite ⟺ (n+,n−,n0)=(n,0,0);
  2. β is positive semidefinite ⟺ n−=0;
  3. β is negative definite ⟺ (n+,n−,n0)=(0,n,0);
  4. β is negative semidefinite ⟺ n+=0;
  5. β is indefinite ⟺ n+>0 and n−>0.

thm-form-matrix-determines.title: Forms and Matrices Correspond
thm-form-matrix-determines.html:
Let V be an n-dimensional vector space over F with ordered basis B, and let β be a bilinear form on V with A=[β]B.

  1. For all u,v∈V, β(u,v)=[u]B⊤A[v]B.
  2. A is the only matrix in Mn(F) with this property.
  3. The assignment β↦[β]B is a bijection from the set of bilinear forms on V onto Mn(F), and it respects sums and scalar multiples: [β+γ]B=[β]B+[γ]B and [cβ]B=c[β]B.

thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues.title: Inertia Is the Sign Pattern of the Spectrum
thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues.title_html: Inertia Is the Sign Pattern of the Spectrum
thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric. Then n+(A) is the number of positive eigenvalues of A, counted with multiplicity, n−(A) the number of negative ones, and n0(A) the multiplicity of 0.

thm-lorentz-boost-form.title: Classification of the Plane Lorentz Transformations
thm-lorentz-boost-form.title_html: Classification of the Plane Lorentz Transformations
thm-lorentz-boost-form.html: Let P∈O(1,1), that is, P∈M2(R) with P⊤diag(1,−1)P=diag(1,−1). Then there are a unique t∈R and unique signs ε,μ∈{1,−1} with P=(εcosh⁡tμsinh⁡tsinh⁡tεμcosh⁡t), and detP=μ. Writing D=diag(1,−1), this says O(1,1)={Bt,BtD,−Bt,−BtD:t∈R}, a disjoint union of four families. Moreover BsBt=Bs+t for all s,t, so {Bt:t∈R} is a subgroup of O(1,1) isomorphic to (R,+).

thm-polarization-forms.title: Polarization
thm-polarization-forms.html: Let charF≠2. The map β↦q, q(v)=β(v,v), is a bijection from the set of symmetric bilinear forms on V onto the set of quadratic forms on V. Its inverse is given by either of β(u,v)=12(q(u+v)−q(u)−q(v))=14(q(u+v)−q(u−v)). In particular a symmetric form is determined by its quadratic form: if β(v,v)=β′(v,v) for all v, then β=β′.

thm-reversed-triangle-inequality.title: Reversed Triangle Inequality
thm-reversed-triangle-inequality.html: Let x,y∈R1,3 be timelike and both future-pointing. Then x+y is timelike and future-pointing, and τ(x+y)≥τ(x)+τ(y), with equality if and only if y is a positive multiple of x.

thm-second-derivative-test.title: The Second-Derivative Test
thm-second-derivative-test.html:
Let f be a real-valued function, twice continuously differentiable on an open set U⊆Rn, let a∈U be a critical point of f, and let (n+,n−,n0) be the inertia of Hf(a). Then:

  1. if Hf(a) is positive definite, that is (n+,n−,n0)=(n,0,0), then a is a strict local minimum of f;
  2. if Hf(a) is negative definite, that is (n+,n−,n0)=(0,n,0), then a is a strict local maximum of f;
  3. if Hf(a) is indefinite, that is n+>0 and n−>0, then a is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum: every neighborhood of a contains points where f>f(a) and points where f<f(a). Such an a is a saddle point.

If n0>0 and a is not covered by (a)–(c), the test gives no information.

thm-sylvester-inertia.title: Sylvester’s Law of Inertia
thm-sylvester-inertia.html: Let β be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V with dim⁡V=n, and let B and B′ be two orthogonal bases for β. Let (n+,n−,n0) be the numbers of positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of [β]B, and (n+′,n−′,n0′) the corresponding numbers for [β]B′. Then n+=n+′,n−=n−′,n0=n0′.

thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition.title: Symmetric Plus Alternating
thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition.html: Let charF≠2 and let β be a bilinear form on V. Then there are a unique symmetric form βs and a unique alternating form βa on V with β=βs+βa, namely βs(u,v)=12(β(u,v)+β(v,u)),βa(u,v)=12(β(u,v)−β(v,u)). In matrices: A=12(A+A⊤)+12(A−A⊤).

thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable.title: Diagonalization of a Symmetric Form
thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable.html:
Let F be a field with charF≠2, let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let β be a symmetric bilinear form on V. Then V has an orthogonal basis for β.

Equivalently: every symmetric A∈Mn(F) is congruent to a diagonal matrix, that is, there is an invertible P∈Mn(F) with P⊤AP diagonal.

thm-symplectic-standard-form.title: Standard Form of an Alternating Form
thm-symplectic-standard-form.title_html: Standard Form of an Alternating Form
thm-symplectic-standard-form.html:
Let F be any field, let V be a vector space over F with dim⁡V=n, and let β be an alternating bilinear form on V. Then there are an integer m≥0 with 2m≤n and a basis B=(u1,…,um,w1,…,wm,z1,…,zn−2m) of V such that, for all i,j, β(ui,wj)=δij,β(ui,uj)=β(wi,wj)=0, and β(zk,v)=0 for every k and every v∈V. Equivalently, in this basis

[β]B=Ω2m⊕0n−2m,Ω2m:=(0Im−Im0).{#eq-standard-alternating-matrix}

In particular:

  1. every alternating A∈Mn(F) is congruent to Ω2m⊕0n−2m for exactly one m;
  2. if β is non-degenerate then n=2m is even and [β]B=Ωn.

thm-witt-decomposition.title: Witt Decomposition
thm-witt-decomposition.html: Let charF≠2 and let β be a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V. Then there are an integer m≥0, hyperbolic planes H1,…,Hm⊆V and a subspace V0⊆V such that V=H1⊥H2⊥⋯⊥Hm⊥V0 and β restricted to V0 is anisotropic. In particular dim⁡V=2m+dim⁡V0.

thm-witt-extension.title: Witt’s Extension Theorem
thm-witt-extension.html: Let F be a field with charF≠2, let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let β be a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form on V. Let U,U′⊆V be subspaces and let σ:U→U′ be an isometry for the restricted forms. Then there is an isometry φ of V with φ|U=σ.
